title: De Blasio re-elected New York mayor in widely anticipated win
text: Bill de Blasio, the Democratic mayor of New York City, won a decisive victory on Tuesday in his effort to secure a second four-year term running the biggest city in the United States. With more than 75 percent of the city's voting precincts reporting, de Blasio, 56, had taken nearly 65 percent of the vote, a margin of 35 percentage points over his Republican rival, state Assemblywoman Nicole Malliotakis, according to New York City's Board of Elections. The New York Times and other media outlets called the race for de Blasio. De Blasio had held a comfortable lead in opinion polls in the run-up to Election Day and had been widely expected to cruise to victory in a city of 8.5 million people where Democratic voters dominate. A progressive liberal, de Blasio campaigned in the past week alongside U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, an independent. Sanders supported de Blasio's call to raise taxes on city residents earning more than $500,000 a year, a proposal with little chance of getting through the state legislature in Albany. The mayor has cast himself as one of the most vocal critics of Republican President Donald Trump, who has drawn strong disapproval ratings from voters in his native city. Daisy Taberas, 71, who immigrated from Peru 48 years ago, said she voted for de Blasio because she was concerned about Trump's stance on immigration. “I like the way (de Blasio) works with children in the schools, and he’s trying to protect the city and he cares about immigration,” Taberas said after casting her ballot at a polling site in Manhattan. De Blasio has come under fire over problems in the city's aging subway system, the largest in the United States.

title: Snapchat once again on the wrong side of a racial lens
text: Through its lens tool, Snapchat lets some 150 million daily users alter reality and play with identity in ways that verge on the absurd. You can turn yourself into a pineapple, a dog or a character that would fit in a Roy Lichtenstein painting. The lenses are blunt tools that produce more than 30 million enhanced selfies a day, and any missteps quickly become part of the public record. Snapchat lenses have been criticized before, amid accusations that the app was promoting blackface or encouraging whitened skin tones as a beauty ideal. So when it pushed a lens to some users this week that gave them slanted eyes, distorted teeth and puffy cheeks, some critics called it a racist caricature of Asian people, or “yellowface.” They also wondered whether these repeated controversies pointed to a larger problem with diversity at the company. The news and the outrage spread widely on Wednesday, with reports by The Verge and Motherboard, a day after Snapchat said it had dismantled the feature. The company offered an explanation: the lens was intended as an homage to anime characters, not as a caricature of Asian people. But for observers who have experienced racism, the lens recalled hurtful stereotypes in action, and others flatly rejected the anime comparison. In an email, Grace Sparapani, an art student whose tweet about the photos was widely shared, said that the lens was “hurtful and uncomfortable to say the least.” She added that “it’s hard to argue with the side by side comparison of the very gross Asian caricature and the filter’s effects. It shows that the filter isn’t just yellowface, but yellowface taken to its derogatory extreme.” Snapchat is not the only company to have crossed these cultural tripwires.

title: Independence Days: My Imperfectly Perfect Gap Year
text: Halfway through an unremarkable freshman year at the University of San Diego, I phoned my parents and told them I intended to leave school after the spring semester. They took it fairly well, considering they had just paid more than $50,000 in tuition and living expenses at one of the ritziest private universities in the country, a place where the gym is named after the dietitian Jenny Craig and some dorms have an ocean view. There, you could easily graduate without knowing that an estimated 1 in 10 students at the nearby California State universities is homeless. I listened to my father's objections while walking to the west edge of campus, past the university's big whitewashed buildings, its meditation garden and its infinity pool, until I reached a spot where I could see all of San Diego's Mission Bay and, beyond it, the Pacific. “If you leave now,” my father said, “you’ll never go back.” He asked me to get the school's permission so that I could come back after a year, and I agreed. That turned my departure into a gap year, something I hadn't considered until then. Many other Americans hadn't either, until the White House announced that President Obama's oldest daughter, Malia, would take one before starting at Harvard next fall. In their coverage of Malia's decision, conservative and liberal media alike called out the perceived elitism of gap years. “Malia Obama Taking a Gap Year Is the Ultimate Sign of Luxury” read the The New York Post headline. “Malia Obama’s ‘Gap Year’ Is Part of a Growing (and Expensive) Trend,” said The New York Times. Slate asked the question “Gap Years for Everyone?”

title: Federal judge upholds Virginia voter ID law
text: A U.S. federal judge on Thursday upheld a 2013 Virginia law that requires prospective voters to present an approved photo identification before casting their ballots. The state's Democratic Party had challenged the law, which was signed by former Republican Governor Robert McDonnell, arguing that it was politically motivated and designed to discourage young and minority voters from turning out on Election Day. “The court’s mission is to judge not the wisdom of the Virginia voter ID law, but rather its constitutionality,” U.S. District Judge Henry Hudson wrote in his decision. Although he acknowledged that the measure created an “inconvenience” for potential voters without drivers' licenses or other government-issued ID, he said that this was not enough to strike it down. “While the merits of this voter identification law, and indeed all aspects of Virginia’s voting regime, can be reasonably debated, it remains true that Virginia has created a scheme of laws to accommodate all people in their right to vote,” Hudson wrote. In a filing, lawyers representing the state Democratic Party said the Republican-dominated state legislature had passed the photo ID law “to stall, if not reverse, the growing success of the Democratic Party in Virginia.” The state argued that ID was needed to ensure that only registered voters cast ballots and to prevent voter fraud. In 2008, President Barack Obama became the first Democrat in more than 40 years to carry Virginia, partly because of turnout among black, Latino and young voters. Obama won the state again in 2012. In the most recent statewide elections, Democrats also swept all of the top offices: governor, lieutenant governor and attorney general. In addition, both of the state's U.S. senators are Democrats.

title: Turkish court orders two detained over U.S. court case, CNN Turk says
text: A Turkish court has issued detention warrants for two people, including a former opposition lawmaker, on suspicion of supplying fake evidence and documents to a court case in the United States, the private broadcaster CNN Turk said on Tuesday. CNN Turk named the two wanted individuals as Aykan Erdemir, a former lawmaker for the Republican People's Party (CHP), and banking auditor Osman Zeki Canitez. It said both were named on a witness list presented for the U.S. trial of former Halkbank executive Mehmet Hakan Atilla. The media relations office of the Istanbul prosecutor's office said it had no information about the detention warrants. U.S. authorities charged Turkish-Iranian gold trader Reza Zarrab and eight other people, including Turkey's former economy minister and three executives of Turkish state-owned Halkbank, with carrying out transactions worth hundreds of millions of dollars for Iran's government and Iranian entities from 2010 to 2015 in a scheme to evade U.S. sanctions. Mehmet Hakan Atilla, who has pleaded not guilty, will be the only person on trial in the U.S. case. U.S. District Judge Richard Berman told potential jurors on Monday that Zarrab, the focus of the case, will not go on trial this week. Atilla and Zarrab are the only two defendants arrested by U.S. authorities. Turkish authorities have said that some evidence presented by prosecutors was fabricated for political motives, and state media reported two weeks ago that authorities had opened an investigation into the prosecutors who brought the U.S. case. Halkbank and Turkish officials have said all of the bank's transactions were fully compliant with national and international regulations, but investors are worried. At 1100 GMT, shares in Turkey's state-owned lender Halkbank were trading 4.47 percent lower at 8.97 lira.

title: Trump lifts Obama-era limits on military equipment transfers to police
text: U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order revoking restrictions placed by his predecessor, Barack Obama, on transferring surplus military equipment to local law enforcement agencies, the White House said. Obama had scaled back the equipment transfer program after law enforcement officers using military-style armored vehicles and guns confronted protesters in Ferguson, Missouri, in 2014 following the fatal police shooting of a black teenager. Trump's executive order said, “All executive departments and agencies are directed, as of the date of this order and consistent with Federal law, to cease implementing those recommendations and, if necessary, to take prompt action to rescind any rules, regulations, guidelines, or policies implementing them.” Since taking office in January, the Republican president has reversed or cut back many of the policies of his Democratic predecessor. The use of military equipment in Ferguson sparked a broader outcry over the use of war-fighting equipment by local law enforcement agencies in the United States. Following a review, Obama barred the military from transferring certain kinds of equipment to police or sheriff's departments, including tracked armored vehicles, armed aircraft or vehicles of any kind, .50-caliber firearms and ammunition, grenade launchers, bayonets and camouflage uniforms. Obama also required law enforcement agencies to justify their need for items such as helicopters and other aircraft, wheeled armored vehicles, unmanned drones, riot helmets and “flash-bang” grenades. “These restrictions that had been imposed went too far,” U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions told a meeting of the Fraternal Order of Police union in Nashville, Tennessee, earlier on Monday. “We will not put superficial concerns above public safety. We will do our best to get you what you need.” Sessions did not say what those superficial concerns were.

title: Russia sanctions bill still stuck in U.S. Congress
text: U.S. lawmakers said on Monday they did not know when a bill imposing new sanctions on Russia might be brought to a vote in the House of Representatives, while the White House said it had concerns about the measure. The bill cleared the Senate by a nearly unanimous margin two weeks ago, and appeared likely to complicate President Donald Trump's wish for warmer relations with Moscow, where officials have condemned new sanctions. A White House official said the Trump administration believed some provisions in the bill would interfere with its ability to use sanctions to try to influence Russia. “There are some provisions in the Senate bill that would unprecedentedly impair Treasury’s ability to wield its sanctions tools, risk endangering the transatlantic sanctions coalition, and weaken the State Department’s ability to credibly signal that we would calibrate our sanctions in response to Russian behavior,” the official said in an emailed statement, asking not to be named. Republican Senator Bob Corker, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and a co-author of the bill, said he hoped for progress within the next day or two on a procedural problem that has kept the House from taking up the Countering Iran's Destabilizing Activities Act, which also contains the new sanctions against Russia. The measure has to pass the House, where Trump's fellow Republicans have a larger majority than in the Senate, before it can be sent to Trump to be signed into law or vetoed. House Republican leaders said last week that the Senate bill violated a constitutional requirement that any bill affecting government revenues must originate in the House, which is known as a “blue slip” violation.

title: Americans want a third option to Trump and Clinton, Reuters/Ipsos poll shows
text: Demand among Americans for an alternative to the two main presidential candidates has risen sharply since the last election, a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll shows, highlighting how unpopular Republican Donald Trump and Democrat Hillary Clinton are. Based on 2,153 interviews, the poll results released on Friday point to strong potential for a third-party candidate, such as Gary Johnson of the Libertarian Party or Jill Stein of the Green Party, to win enough of the vote in the Nov. 8 presidential election to affect its outcome. According to the July 1-8 poll, 21 percent of likely voters will not support Trump or Clinton. That compares with about 13 percent of likely voters who rejected the two main options at the same stage of the 2012 race between incumbent President Barack Obama and Republican challenger Mitt Romney. The poll also found that a majority of American voters have an overall “unfavorable” view of both main candidates, with 46 percent of Clinton supporters and 47 percent of Trump supporters saying their top priority in voting will be to keep the opposing candidate out of the White House. Demand for an alternative could prove decisive in fiercely contested battleground states. In Florida in 2012, for example, Obama won by less than 1 percentage point. If this year's race is equally close, third-party candidates could draw enough support to swing the state from one major party to the other. Even so, Johnson and Stein both face a problem that makes their influence hard to predict: most voters still do not know who they are. Among likely voters, 23 percent say they are at least “somewhat familiar” with Johnson, a former governor of New Mexico. That falls to 16 percent for Stein, a physician. Johnson could appeal to both liberals and conservatives.

title: Researchers cast doubt on cause of Chilean poet Neruda's death
text: International researchers looking into the death of Chilean poet Pablo Neruda on Friday questioned whether he died of cancer 44 years ago as had been assumed, and did not rule out foul play. Neruda, famous for his passionate love poems and firm communist views, died days after a coup in September 1973 that brought in the brutal dictatorship of Augusto Pinochet. Neruda's chauffeur has claimed that Pinochet's agents exploited the poet's illness to inject poison into his stomach while he lay in hospital. Neruda's body was exhumed in 2013, and earlier tests have found no evidence of poison, although testing continues. Spanish forensic specialist Aurelio Luna of the University of Murcia told journalists that his team had found something that could possibly be a laboratory-cultivated bacteria. It will be analyzed, with results expected in six months to a year. Luna also said tests showed that death from prostate cancer was unlikely at the moment Neruda died. “From analysis of the data we cannot accept that the poet had been in an imminent situation of death at the moment of entering the hospital,” he said. “We cannot confirm if the nature of Pablo Neruda's death was natural or violent,” he added. Pinochet died in 2006. Neruda's family and supporters have been split over whether the case should be closed and his remains returned to his grave near his coastal home of Isla Negra, or whether researchers should keep carrying out tests.
